title: The summit
hook: the path goes on after the hill: every day's prayer is another step
tomorrow: the hill is climbed. what does day one look like the second time?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the view from the top: every path in sight, every one turned toward one point. Everything faces him. Today, the last step of the climb, and what comes after it.
screen: `EVERYTHING FACES HIM.` → `THE LAST STEP, AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: A gym in January. A new notebook. The first clean page of a planner. People love a fresh start. At an airport curb, a friend pulls over, pops the trunk, and before the suitcase is even out, holds up her phone: a text from her grandmother, for the flight. It's the line her grandmother says over coffee every morning, from the Bible: his compassions fail not; they are new every morning. Read it twice. Because the path you've climbed has its own word for mornings, and for what you do once you reach the top.
screen: `A FRESH START.` → `A TEXT AT THE CURB.` → `NEW EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the question at the summit: when you've finished, what then? The Qur'an answers in two short verses, in Pickthall's words: "So when thou art relieved, still toil And strive to please thy Lord." Finished one thing? Turn to the next. And elsewhere: serve your Lord until the certainty comes to you, which commentators read as death. There's no finish line short of that. Remember the delayed gate and the jacket on the carpet, back at the start of this camp: the Prophet ﷺ said the deeds God loves most are the constant ones, even if small. So the summit isn't a flag. It's a prayer that begins again: Allahu akbar, the Fatiha, bow, prostrate, rise, the same steps you learned at the bottom of the hill. Now the neighbor, in their own words. That text at the curb comes from Lamentations, in the Bible that Jews and Christians share. In the King James words: "his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." The shared thing is real, and it's worth telling a friend tonight: both traditions refuse to let an ending be the end. Mercy renews; you begin again. And the honest difference: Lamentations is a poet's grief over a ruined Jerusalem, and the newness it sings belongs to God's faithfulness, found in the ashes. The Qur'an's verse speaks to someone who has just finished well, and tells them: still toil.
screen: `WHEN YOU'RE DONE, STILL TOIL.` · `NO FINISH LINE SHORT OF THE END.` · `NEW EVERY MORNING.` · `GRIEF AND FAITHFULNESS; WORK AND STRIVING.` · then, large: `AND BEGIN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: If you pray, pray two units now, and let the first Allahu akbar be your day one, again. If you don't, stand for a moment, then sit, and let that be your first step. Either way, before the time is up, name the first small thing you'll do tomorrow morning, and where in the morning it goes.
screen: `TWO UNITS, OR ONE STANDING BREATH.` · `DAY ONE, AGAIN.` · `TOMORROW'S FIRST SMALL THING.`

segments.voice: The summit: the top of the hill, where the path doesn't end. It turns, and starts again at the first step.
Your line: and begin again, from the very first Allahu akbar. Fifteen of fifteen, the summit, and the path goes on.

howItsDone: Muslims pray every day for life, beginning each prayer with 'Allahu akbar'; on finishing a reading of the whole Qur'an, many begin again, and after Ramadan many keep a little of its practice going.
